modelName: Ostrom x eVSM crosswalk banded by IAD level
modelNote: Left column: Ostrom / Jones conditions. Right column: eVSM functions. Bands are Ostrom's levels of rule-making; the small italic line on each node is its Markov-blanket role. Solid teal = strong match, dashed teal = partial, blue dashed lines into the dot = Ostrom variables carried by the informal OU-OU channels, orange = eVSM changes agreed in this discussion. The sphere-to-sphere mesh and the environment couplings are in the as-drawn version. Sources: Jones (2003) redrawing of Ostrom's origins, survival and performance model; Marc Pierson's eVSM plus environment for RCN. Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5.5 · September 2026.

nodes.note:
environment; Ostrom right panel

OSTROM FRAMES · Outside the group's own rules. Principle 7 (recognition of rights) and principle 8 (nested enterprises) can only be read here, from other bodies' rules: the city's ordinance, the landowner's lease, the larger council's charter. Code those too, or these two principles stay 'can't tell'.
nodes.label: OUTSIDE  ·  environment; Ostrom right panel

nodes.note:
who may make the rules · eVSM magenta

OSTROM FRAMES · Level test: does it change who may change the rules? Then it is constitutional, the most leverage. All seven rule types work here: boundary says who counts as a member, position creates the seats, choice says what each seat may do, aggregation says how the rule-makers decide, information says who sees the charter, payoff says what membership costs and gives, scope says what the rule-makers may touch. In the grammar, most sentences here are creating agreements: WHAT ARE WE CREATING?, FORMED?, OUT OF WHAT?
nodes.label: CONSTITUTIONAL  ·  who may make the rules · eVSM magenta

nodes.note:
System 4, in both levels · eVSM purple

OSTROM FRAMES · System 4 spans two levels, and so do sentences about it. Read the level from the sentence's TO WHAT?: acting on the rules is collective choice; acting on who makes the rules is constitutional.
nodes.label: BRIDGE  ·  System 4, in both levels · eVSM purple

nodes.note:
rules in use and the budget · eVSM red, System 3

OSTROM FRAMES · Level test: does it change a rule? Then it is collective choice. Principle 3 lives in this whole band, and the rule types split it into five questions. Are the people affected seated (boundary)? Is there a seat for them (position, set one band up)? Do they see proposals in time (information)? Does their voice count, by vote, consent, or only by being asked (aggregation)? What may they change (scope)? A group can fail any one of the five while saying it follows principle 3.
nodes.label: COLLECTIVE CHOICE  ·  rules in use and the budget · eVSM red, System 3

nodes.note:
Coordination and shared services · eVSM teal and blue

OSTROM FRAMES · Level test: does it change a number? Then it is operational, the least leverage, where most effort goes. The seven rule types here govern the work: who may use, which roles do what, what each must or must not do, who hears what, who pays and who receives.
nodes.label: OPERATIONAL: functions  ·  Coordination and shared services · eVSM teal and blue

nodes.note:
operating units, each a nested blanket

OSTROM FRAMES · Each operating unit is a whole commons with its own levels inside it. That is principle 8's sense of 'nested' (bodies inside bodies), which is different from the levels of rule-making in the bands above.
nodes.label: OPERATIONAL: the users  ·  operating units, each a nested blanket

nodes.note: The most organized actor outside the group, and the one with the longest reach — five red arrows leave here. It can grant legal standing and local prerogative, back local sanctions, fund monitoring technology, and speed information. Or withhold all of it.
nodes.label: Governmental Agencies

nodes.note: A federated tier above the local group. Jones (upper right of Figure 1): informational and motivational resources, technical training, help with conflict management and compliance, assured certainty of ownership status, and appropriate legal recourse.
nodes.label: Larger System of Institutional Support

nodes.note: Shocks from outside: markets, migration, climate, technology, war. They matter less in themselves than in the pace at which they arrive.
nodes.label: Exogenous Changes

nodes.note:
RIGHT PANEL — everything outside the user group and its institution. Jones: these supply the bulk of the influence on survival, and reach origin and performance only indirectly, feeding through the center and left panels.

OSTROM FRAMES · Principle 2A, fit with local conditions, sits here. It is the one principle no rule and no coded sentence can show: whether the rules suit this place is a judgment about the place. Evidence comes from practice only: ask the people under the rules, watch the resource over time.
nodes.label: External Factors

nodes.note: The survival condition Ostrom names as non-rapid change. An institution absorbs change it has time to learn from; the same change arriving fast outruns rule-making and the organization dies.
nodes.label: Rate of Change

nodes.note: The larger viable system this one is an operating unit of. Added for the crosswalk.
nodes.label: Next recursion up

nodes.note:
Clear boundaries on who belongs. Without a known membership there is no one for a common understanding to be common among.

OSTROM FRAMES · Principle 1 is two rules, not one. 1A, user boundaries, is a boundary rule: who is in. 1B, resource boundaries, is a scope rule: what the shared thing is. They fail separately. In the grammar, look for a creating agreement for the members (WHAT ARE WE CREATING?, FORMED?, OUT OF WHAT?). A rule about 'gardeners' with no sentence creating gardeners is a gap the checker finds.
nodes.label: Recognized Membership

nodes.note:
A shared reading of who may withdraw what. Jones spends a page on what kind of thing this is: not a structure, but information storage with a comparator inside it — a store that slowly develops over time AND a device that compares new information against what is already known. It then feeds decision-making costs — Jones calls that a switch — which is how everything the users know finally reaches Origin.

OSTROM FRAMES · Common understanding is where rules in use live. Coding records rules on paper; this store records what people actually expect of each other. The difference is the subject matter, findable only by observation.
nodes.label: Common Understanding

nodes.note:
Whether the rules people actually follow are the rules the state recognizes. A gap between practice and law leaves the group enforcing rules no court will uphold.

OSTROM FRAMES · Rules in form versus rules in use. The grammar's OR ELSE decides a sentence's strength: all five parts make an agreed rule; no OR ELSE makes a shared expectation; no OR ELSE and no MUST or MAY makes a shared habit. In real documents the OR ELSE is usually empty, and a sentence without one drifts.
nodes.label: de facto vs. de jure

nodes.note:
Whether the group is legally recognized and free to make its own rules. Granted from outside (red — it comes from government) but it works inside: it changes what strategies users believe are open to them.

OSTROM FRAMES · Principle 7, recognition of rights. A scope rule, but written by an outside body, so it is only partly readable from the group's own text. The checker would ask: what gives the group the right to make these rules?
nodes.label: Legal Status, Local Perogative

nodes.note:
S-11. Constitutional level, tuning layer. Identity and the shared model.

OSTROM FRAMES · Beneath the constitutional level is the metaconstitutional one: what people believe is even thinkable. It is unwritten, which is why it is the strongest. The grammar reaches it only as shared habits, recorded when seen in practice, with nothing written behind them.
nodes.label: Worldview & Identity

nodes.note: S-10. Constitutional level, tuning layer. Who may make the rules.
nodes.label: Policies & Legal

nodes.note: What users believe they could do instead. Origin happens only when organizing looks better than the alternatives people can actually see — perceived, not available.
nodes.label: Percieved Alternative Strategies

nodes.note: What the group knows about condition, stock and yield. Splits two ways: into perceived scarcity, and into the store of common understanding.
nodes.label: Info about Resource

nodes.note: S-8. Bridge, internal core.
nodes.label: Planning

nodes.note: S-9. Bridge between collective choice and constitutional, sensory / motor. Carries traffic between Policies & Legal and the Regulators, so the blanket holds.
nodes.label: Research

nodes.note:
What it costs the group to reach and revise agreement. Jones reads it as a switch: it gates origin, and it is one of only two factors reaching performance directly, the other being enforcement costs. What it costs is set upstream by group size and by how unequally assets are held.

OSTROM FRAMES · Aggregation is the rule type no design principle names. Principles 3 and 6 assume decisions get made but never say how choices combine: majority, consent, consensus, single authority, whoever showed up. The aggregation rule sets most of what deciding costs. Ask: who has to agree for this to count?
nodes.label: Decision -making Costs

nodes.note:
Rules few enough and plain enough to be known, taught, and checked. Ostrom refined this to Jones in 2002 (personal communication): really the 'smallest and simplest set of rules relevant to the variety in the environment' — simple relative to the environment, not simple absolutely.

OSTROM FRAMES · In the grammar, one sentence holds exactly one MUST, MAY, or MUST NOT. Counting coded sentences at each level is the plain measure of 'small': a commons with operational rules and none above them can follow its rules but cannot change them.
nodes.label: Small, Simple Set of Rules

nodes.note:
What it costs to detect and sanction violations. This is the center panel's one direct line into performance: rules too expensive to enforce eat the benefit they were meant to protect.

OSTROM FRAMES · Principle 5, graduated sanctions. A payoff rule: the OR ELSE. In the grammar, look for several OR ELSE sentences on the same rule whose WHEN answers step up: a first breach, a second, a third. One sanction for every breach is the gap.
nodes.label: Enforcement Costs

nodes.note:
Local rules enforced by users AND backed by external authority. Two levels beat one: the group sees the violation, the state makes the sanction stick.

OSTROM FRAMES · In the grammar, enforcement is a 'backed by' chain. Follow it: the sanction leads to someone's duty to carry it out, the duty to the creating agreement for that role, and its OUT OF WHAT? to whom the role answers. Dual enforcement is the chain reaching an outside body.
nodes.label: Dual Enforcement

nodes.note:
How wealth and holdings are distributed among users. Heterogeneity here decides who gains from a rule and who pays for it — the question Jones's dissertation was built on. Feeds two ways: into interdependence, and into what the group's decisions cost it.

OSTROM FRAMES · Principle 2B, costs in proportion to benefits. A payoff rule, matched against choice: for each benefit a group grants (MAY water), a duty from the same WHO (MUST give work hours), scaling with the benefit.
nodes.label: Asset Structure

nodes.note: S-5. Collective-choice level, tuning layer.
nodes.label: Innovation

nodes.note: S-6. Collective-choice level, internal core. Where rules in use and sanctions are decided; manages the superordinate coordination function.
nodes.label: Managing

nodes.note: S-7. Collective-choice level, sensory / motor. The budget: taxes collected and redistributed. Also measurement, facing outward to Financiers and Suppliers.
nodes.label: Resources & Accounting

nodes.note:
Low-cost arenas for settling disputes. The one place in the model with a two-way link: shared understanding makes disputes settleable, and settling disputes rebuilds shared understanding.

OSTROM FRAMES · Principle 6, conflict resolution, a collective-choice arrangement. Three rule types: position (a venue: mediator, meeting, council), boundary (who may bring a dispute, and when), aggregation (how it gets settled). Ask too: where does a dispute about the rules themselves go?
nodes.label: Conflict Resolution

nodes.note:
Being able to watch, or hear by gossip, what others take. The observability that makes cooperation checkable. Jones flags a live question here: why is this NOT linked to interdependence/subtractability? Perhaps you don't need to watch your neighbors to know you depend on them — but is that true?

OSTROM FRAMES · Principle 4A, monitoring users. Four parts, each can be missing: a role (position), a duty to watch (choice), reports back to the users (information), and someone the monitor answers to (constitutional: the role's OUT OF WHAT?).
nodes.label: Info on Other's Resource Use

nodes.note: How fast users learn the state of the resource. Both monitoring technology and government agencies act here — the lag, not the data, is the variable.
nodes.label: Speed of Access to Info

nodes.note:
Instruments and methods that make the condition of the resource observable. Cheap monitoring is what makes a small set of rules enforceable at all.

OSTROM FRAMES · Principle 4B, monitoring the resource. An information rule. In the grammar, a WHEN such as 'when the tank is below half' assumes someone reads the tank; if no sentence gives anyone that duty, the text itself shows the gap. The readings over time are where SPC charts belong.
nodes.label: Technology for Monitoring Resources

nodes.note: S-1. Operational level, tuning layer. Beer: coordination runs both directly between operating units and through a superordinate coordination function that Managing (S-6) runs, hence the agreed S-1 to S-6 link. Proposed: also carries peer monitoring (the watching, not the sanctioning).
nodes.label: Coordination

nodes.note: S-2. Operational level (shared service bridging S-3 and the operating units), tuning layer.
nodes.label: HR

nodes.note: S-3. Operational level (shared service), internal core.
nodes.label: Infrastructure / Tools

nodes.note: S-4. Operational level (shared service), sensory / motor.
nodes.label: Outreach

nodes.note: Upstream of nearly everything social in this map. Size sets how much trust is possible, whether open communication happens on its own, and what it costs to decide together. Jones's own research is on group heterogeneity's effect on cooperation (Jones 2002).
nodes.label: Group Size

nodes.note: The left panel's focal process and the paper's main unfinished business. Jones argues trust is not one thing but several: in-group/out-group standing, a history of mutually beneficial transactions over time, the ability to watch others or hear about them, and relative power and economic status. The trust 'switch' may need several different triggers. And it is the one place the outputs reach back into: survival feeds trust, so a group that has held together is easier to trust than one that has not.
nodes.label: Trust

nodes.note: Talk among users. Talk is what turns options each member holds privately into a strategy the group can perceive jointly.
nodes.label: Open Communication

nodes.note: Shared background, language, livelihood. Ostrom's 'lack of cultural antagonisms' (1992:302-303) — a precondition for both trust and easy talk.
nodes.label: Similarities

nodes.note: Time together and a history of dealing with each other. Builds trust, and separately shapes which alternatives people find realistic — having cooperated before makes cooperating thinkable.
nodes.label: Experience

nodes.note:
The resource fact that makes collective action necessary: what I take, you cannot. Without subtractability there is nothing to govern and no reason to organize.

OSTROM FRAMES · Principle 1B, resource boundaries: is the shared thing defined? A scope rule. In the grammar, the TO WHAT? of the rules should point at a defined resource. A rule about 'the tank' with nothing saying which tank is a gap.
nodes.label: Inter- dependence / subtractability

nodes.note: How far users live from the resource. Jones's own example of the power of indirect effects: distance never touches origin or performance directly — it works through trust and through information on others' use, and only then through common understanding and decision-making costs.
nodes.label: Distance to Resource

nodes.note: Scarcity is what makes interdependence bite. Note the path it arrives on — through information about the resource. Perceived scarcity, not measured scarcity, is what moves a group.
nodes.label: Resource Scarcity

nodes.note: PHASE 1 — the appropriator organization comes into being. Ostrom's first state: whether users facing a shared resource ever form an institution at all. Almost everything feeding it comes from the left panel — who the users are, what the resource does to them, and what it costs them to decide together. It is an end state, not a way station — Jones links none of the three outputs to each other except the one feedback from survival.
nodes.label: Origin

nodes.note: PHASE 3 — equity and efficiency once the institution runs. Sustainability plus a positive benefit:cost ratio, a match between users and members, and knowledge acquired about the resource and its users. This is what users actually want; survival is only the price of admission — which is why survival feeds back into it.
nodes.label: Performance

nodes.note: PHASE 2 — the organization persists. Turns on rule enforcement, legitimacy borrowed from other institutions, and change that is not too rapid. Jones: survival is not really the goal of most institutions — origin and performance are. The one output that feeds back into the model: into performance, and all the way back across the canvas into trust.
nodes.label: Survival

nodes.note: The whole eVSM holding together. Added for the crosswalk; neither diagram has it as a node.
nodes.label: Viability
eVSM FOR RCN: functions and environment
HOW TO READ ONE RULE  ·  hover
nodes.note:
How to read one rule: the Institutional Grammar. It sits outside the map because it describes one sentence, not the system.

A rule about what people do answers WHEN? WHO? MUST, MAY, OR MUST NOT? DO WHAT? TO WHAT? HOW? OR ELSE? A creating agreement answers WHAT ARE WE CREATING? MUST OR MAY? FORMED? OUT OF WHAT?

ADICO (Crawford and Ostrom 1995) is the older form: Attribute, Deontic, aIm, Condition, Or else. IG 2.0 (Frantz and Siddiki 2021) splits Condition into WHEN and HOW, adds TO WHAT, creating agreements, and nesting.

The grammar feeds the map: DO WHAT? mostly gives the rule type, TO WHAT? mostly gives the band, OR ELSE gives the strength. The design principles are questions asked of all the coded sentences together. Full text: FedWiki page 'How The Ostrom Frames Fit Together'.

edges.note: Informal channel between every pair of operating units (Marc will redraw the eVSM this way).
edges.tripleNotes: Where most of the variety is handled (Marc). Ostrom's social variables live on these channels, not in any sphere.

edges.note: Informal channel, return direction.
Beer's superordinate coordination, run by System 3. Agreed; exact drawing still to decide.
Return direction of the S-1 to S-6 link.
Jones's most organized outside actor is the eVSM's Regulators. It reaches the eVSM only through Research (S-9), which is what the Markov blanket requires.
Shocks from outside: in the eVSM they arrive through the environment column, here competitors.
Shocks from outside: markets and places shifting.

Beer: viability is adapting at the rate the environment changes. Ostrom's non-rapid change is the same condition. Free-energy reading: change outruns the model's updating, so surprise cannot be brought down.
edges.label: adapt as fast as the world changes

edges.note:
Ostrom's nested enterprises (design principle 8) are Beer's recursion: this commons is one operating unit of a larger viable system, with its own metasystem and blanket.

OSTROM FRAMES · Principle 8, nested enterprises: boundary and position rules linking a body to the larger one it belongs to ('the garden sends one delegate to the neighborhood council'). Two senses of 'nested': principle 8 means bodies inside bodies; the bands mean levels of rule-making inside any one body. Each body in the nest has its own bands.
edges.label: nesting = recursion

edges.note: Training, equipment and help with conflicts also arrive from partners at the same level.
Clear boundaries (design principle 1) are the system's identity: who is inside. In blanket terms, where the blanket is.
Jones: an information store with a comparator inside it. That is a prior plus a prediction-error signal, the core of free-energy minimization, carried in the tuning layer.
edges.label: store + comparator = prior + error

edges.note: Also the shared model of self and environment that Beer places in System 4.
And the model Planning works from.
Legal standing is set at the constitutional level. Marc: S-9 carries the traffic between S-10 and Regulators, so no direct S-10 to Regulators edge.
Whether the rules in use are the rules the state recognizes: a constitutional question, answered in Policies & Legal, informed through Research.
Options the group can see: Planning.
And the options it can invent: Innovation.
Knowledge of the resource and its condition: sensing.
Marc's S-7 as measurement: the resource counted.

Ostrom's 2002 wording, the smallest and simplest set of rules relevant to the variety in the environment, is Ashby's law, and free energy's complexity against accuracy trade-off. Rules in use are made in the collective-choice arena.
edges.label: requisite variety

edges.note: Bounded by the constitutional rules above.
The cost of detecting and sanctioning. Sanctions stay here, not in Coordination: combine the watching, not the sanctioning.
And it comes out of the budget.
What it costs to reach and revise collective choices: the cost of running the collective-choice arena.

Unequal holdings decide who gains from a rule and who pays for it. That is the budget: Marc's taxes collected and redistributed. Distributive, not relational, so it sits in a sphere rather than on an edge.

OSTROM FRAMES · Payoff rules. Principle 2B asks that what each member puts in matches what they take out: in the grammar, each MAY (a benefit) matched by a MUST (a duty) with the same WHO.
edges.label: who pays, who receives

edges.note: The local half of enforcement.
The half backed from outside, recognized constitutionally. Also the backstop when peer monitoring fails.

Cheap, local, routine dispute handling is System 2's job: damping oscillation between operating units.

OSTROM FRAMES · Principle 6 at work: a cheap, local venue settles disputes before they swing the whole system. In rule types, a position (the venue) plus an aggregation rule (how it decides).
edges.label: anti-oscillation

edges.note:
Peer monitoring (design principle 4) has the same sideways shape as coordination. Proposed: fold the watching into Coordination and keep sanctions in Managing and Policies & Legal. How to draw inspection is still open.

OSTROM FRAMES · Information rules, not payoff rules. Watching and sanctioning are different rule types; principle 4A needs the first, principle 5 the second, and a group can have one without the other.
edges.label: watching, not sanctioning

edges.note: Instruments that make the resource observable are shared tools.
The delay, not the data, is the variable: tools and channels set it.
And how quickly Coordination hears.
How many operating units the metasystem must absorb: their variety.
Operating units drawing on the same resource: overlapping local environments, which is why they oscillate and need coordination.
How close each operating unit is to its resource.
Scarcity in the local environment the operating units share.
Ostrom's survival is Beer's viability.
edges.label: same concept

edges.note: Performance is what viability buys: Beer measures it with actuality, capability and potentiality.
edges.label: Beer's actuality / capability / potentiality

metaEdges.note: Trust lowers how much each side must check the other: a property of the channel, not of any sphere.
How much the channel can carry.
How little translation the channel needs (Beer's transducers).
Mutually beneficial transactions over time: the history of a two-way channel settling into balance.
What I take, you cannot: the reason the channel carries so much.
Watching what others take travels first over these channels.
